loveday_forster_usage: sound — all sounds arise from the impact of air against bodies or bodies against air; qualitative differences determined by the physical properties of the sound-producing organs and the transmitting air.
notes: Central object of the treatise. Extends the general impact-theory of sound from De Anima II.8 into detailed material acoustics.

loveday_forster_usage: impact — the fundamental mechanism of all sound production; air is set in motion by contraction, expansion, compression, or the blow of breath against bodies.
notes: Central technical term: all sound is caused by πληγή. The force and manner of impact determine sound quality.

loveday_forster_usage: breath — the material cause of vocal sound; its force, quantity, and manner of expulsion from lungs through windpipe and mouth determine qualitative vocal differences.
notes: In De Audibilibus, πνεῦμα = breath (physiological), not the connate spirit (σύμφυτον πνεῦμα) of MA ch. 10.

loveday_forster_usage: clearness — a quality of sound analogous to clearness in colour; produced by concentrated, solid, and pure stimuli striking with maximal penetration.
notes: The clearness analogy across sound and colour is one of the treatise's notable cross-modal claims.

loveday_forster_usage: hard/soft — applied to sounds, voices, lungs, horns, and strings. Hard sounds strike the hearing with force; soft sounds arise from gentle breath. Determined by the force of breath from lungs, not windpipe hardness.
notes: The treatise corrects unnamed opponents who attribute vocal hardness to the windpipe rather than the lungs.

loveday_forster_usage: rough — rough sounds arise when the impact of air is not single but divided and dispersed, each portion striking separately; compared to rough objects touching the skin.
notes: The cross-modal analogy to touch (roughness of sound ~ roughness of surface) supports the common sensibles doctrine.

loveday_forster_usage: concord — musical concords explained by overlapping note-impacts; the shriller note strikes simultaneously with the slower, and intermediate sounds escape notice, producing apparent continuity.
notes: The concord theory in De Audibilibus is more mechanistic (impact-based) than the ratio-theory of Sens. ch. 3.

loveday_forster_usage: shrill/deep — pitch distinction: quickness of breathing produces shrillness; slowness or large breath-quantity produces depth.
notes: Standard Greek terminology for pitch; ὀξύς literally 'sharp', βαρύς literally 'heavy'.

loveday_forster_usage: thick/thin — volume-related: thick sounds produced with great breath-quantity (men's voices, well-filled oboes); thin with small quantity (children, women, eunuchs).
notes: Distinct from pitch (ὀξύς/βαρύς); thickness/thinness concerns the quantity of breath, not its speed.
